title: Mohnish Pabrai Lecture at Peking University (Guanghua School of Mgmt) - Dec 22, 2017
summary: Pabrai lectures Peking University students on the power of compounding, using the stories of the 11-year-old Warren Buffett, the $24 Manhattan purchase, and his own 'Compound 26' license plate. The Q&A covers his exit from the insurance business, why he shifted from the US to India, circle of competence (Buffett's 'too hard' box, John Arrillaga), the stupidity of stop losses, the Delta Financial zero and the checklist, Maotai as his only Chinese holding, and position sizing.

ideas.idea: Take a simple idea and take it seriously; successful people are built on simple ideas pursued with fanatical intensity.
ideas.detail: He opens with Einstein's quote and says that when you study successful people, the core idea is simple and the difference is intense execution, citing the yellow bike-share company at Peking U as an example of a simple idea executed well.

ideas.idea: Buffett's success came from combining a seed-capital engine with an early, fanatical understanding of compounding.
ideas.detail: At 11 in 1941 Buffett read '1000 Ways to Make $1000' and declared he would be a millionaire by 35; by 1965 he was worth $8-9 million. As a teenager he ran the Wilson Coin Operated Machine Company with Don Danley, placing 25 pinball machines in DC barbershops at $15 per machine that paid back in about six weeks, and rented a repaired Rolls-Royce for $100 a weekend.

ideas.idea: The Rule of 72 and the $24 Manhattan story show that a modest 7% return over long enough periods becomes astronomical.
ideas.detail: If the Native Americans had compounded the $24 from 1626 at 7%, doubling every 10 years and adding three zeros per century, they would have about $13 trillion today, versus roughly $100 trillion total US wealth, so they would have come out ahead. He calls the Rule of 72 'elastic math' and says you must train yourself to think geometrically rather than arithmetically.

ideas.idea: Compounding has three variables (starting capital, rate of return, length of runway), and the rate is the only one you truly control, so maximize it and protect your runway by not spending.
ideas.detail: He tells 25-year-old students they have a 65-year runway to age 90, and that a Tesla bought today costs 120 million dollars at 15% over 50 years, so skip the Tesla and even the Starbucks; Buffett declines wine at parties and picks up pennies because every penny is the start of another billion.

ideas.idea: Most of a compounder's wealth arrives late: Buffett's net worth at 50 was one-third of 1% of what it is today, so keep the engine running as long as possible.
ideas.detail: Over 99% of Buffett's wealth came after age 50. Pabrai says 23 of his own 30-year game have passed and most of the money comes at the end, so he has decided not to stop at 60 but to keep going to 80 or 85.

ideas.idea: Pabrai's own game was to turn $1 million into $1 billion in 30 years by doubling every three years, hence the 'Compound 26' license plate.
ideas.detail: After selling part of his IT company in 1994 he had $1 million; 26% a year doubles in three years, and 10 doublings is 1024x. He compounded at over 70% a year from 1995-99 part-time, Pabrai Funds did mid-30s before fees from 1999-2007, fell almost 70% in 2007-09, and is back on track; his $1 million became $170 million despite many zeros.

ideas.idea: Buffett kept changing his method while never changing his focus on compounding; the shift from fair businesses at good prices to good businesses at fair prices came only in his mid-50s.
ideas.detail: He distinguishes understanding compounding (Buffett at 11) from understanding how to compound (Graham at 20), and notes the Munger-influenced quality shift happened when Buffett was 50-60, showing he continuously looks to improve.

ideas.idea: Insurance is a structurally difficult business where your dumbest competitor sets your price and you do not know your product's cost for 5-10 years; he is exiting it for good.
ideas.detail: After three years owning an insurance company he is selling it, having learned that policyholders treat premiums like a tax and shop for the cheapest, that inflation raises future claims paid in future dollars, and that Buffett made it work only because he is an incredible manager. He contrasts it with Maotai, which sells an 800 RMB bottle at a tiny cost, 'a license to print money'.

ideas.idea: Zero management fees are a competitive advantage, and you do not need to be full time or wealthy to run money this way; manage your own money well first to earn the right.
ideas.detail: His fund started in his house with no staff and no expenses; his best five years (1995-2000) were part-time at 10-15 hours a week while running another company. Keep a good job for living expenses and let a small sum compound while convincing others to invest.

ideas.idea: Fish where the fish are: the US has shrunk from 8,000 to under 3,700 public companies while brainpower chasing them has exploded, whereas India has 5,000 listed companies, 4,000 of them followed by nobody.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: In the last two or three years he has found almost nothing in the US, where physics PhDs join hedge funds instead of NASA and mispricing shrinks; India offers a faster-growing economy and huge tailwinds, and he sees China's standard of living as nearly doubled between his 2008 and 2017 visits.

ideas.idea: China is outside his circle of competence, so despite 400% on Maotai he holds only one Chinese stock and will not chase more without help.
ideas.detail: Managing about $870 million, he says if he focused on China he would 'get his head handed to him' because he cannot judge culture, nuances or honesty; there is only one Maotai in the world, and he asks students to send Chinese ideas to mp@pabraifunds.com.

ideas.idea: After 2008 he moved from a 10x10 portfolio to three position sizes of 2%, 5% or 10%, using 2% baskets when a whole sector is cheap and he cannot pick the best name.
ideas.detail: In the crisis the entire commodity sector collapsed, so he put 2% into a number of commodity companies and had no losers. He still prefers 10% positions because too many stocks means you know each less; Maotai started at 3-4% because of culture concerns and has grown to about 10% of the fund.

ideas.idea: Buffett's 'too hard' box, where 98-99% of ideas go, is the model: wait for rare anomalies within your circle of competence and act only then.
ideas.detail: He saw the too-hard box on Buffett's desk during an office tour with Guy Spier. His example is a US steel company at $45 with $15 cash per share, no debt, and contracted earnings of $15 a share for two years; the stock rose to 75, then 90, and he sold at 150 when a buyer emerged.

ideas.idea: John Arrillaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within one mile of Stanford, proving a tiny circle of competence and specialization beat breadth.
ideas.detail: Arrillaga never used much debt, bought when things went down and sold when everyone got euphoric; a Minnesota-only fund similarly beat the market. Having a lot of things to look at is not an advantage; become really good at a few things and wait.

ideas.idea: Buy what is hated and unloved, and judge by the long term rather than one or two quarters.
ideas.detail: He bought an Indian company with a market cap under $100 million earning $50 million a year that the market hated, and bought Maotai when its price fell during the anti-corruption crackdown because government consumption would normalize over time.

ideas.idea: Be a relentlessly curious student: meet companies to learn, not to invest, and go to sleep a little wiser each day as Munger says.
ideas.detail: On his India trip he planned to meet six companies including a housing finance firm with a long list of questions, purely to understand things better when he leaves; once enough data is taken in, occasionally things fit and you can act.

ideas.idea: Stop losses are stupid for a value investor because auction-driven markets fluctuate without regard to underlying value, and those fluctuations are the source of opportunity.
ideas.detail: Indian TV pundits give a target and stop loss for every stock; the market prices Amazon at $1,200 to the cent when even Bezos cannot forecast its cash flows. He bought Maotai at about 170 RMB, it fell to 150 right after, and a stop loss would have taken him out. He uses a Beijing house analogy: a house quoted every six seconds would swing wildly with no change in the asset.

ideas.idea: He never buys anything unless he believes it is worth at least double its price.
ideas.detail: If he buys at 20 RMB it must be worth at least 40; he tells students not to send ideas where 80 RMB is worth 110, only ones where 80 is worth 200 or 300, because everything he buys goes down first and a high compounding rate needs big discounts.

ideas.idea: The number one reason investments fail is leverage; Delta Financial going to zero cost $70 million and led him to create his checklist.
ideas.detail: Delta Financial was a sensibly run mortgage originator that depended on warehouse lines and securitization; when securitization froze in 2008 it violated covenants and collapsed with little equity. He is now skeptical of banks and financial institutions with small equity and large debt.

ideas.idea: With no leverage you can hold through any crash, so seek businesses like Google and Maotai that crank out cash without debt.
ideas.detail: If North Korea launched missiles the market might fall 50-70%, but Maotai consumption would normalize and Stanford real estate would be unaffected long term; you must be positioned to take advantage of such events, never to go to zero, because any number multiplied by zero is zero.

ideas.idea: He works alone with no analysts because a team creates pressure to act; instead he wants the wisdom of crowds, a million analysts sending him ideas.
ideas.detail: A stranger in Canada sent him an elegant write-up on an Indian stock trading at one-tenth of value; after three hours of fact-checking he invested the maximum allowed ($20 million, under 10% of a sub-$200 million company) and it rose 10x in two and a half years. A smart hired analyst would bring ideas outside his circle and he would eventually feel obliged to buy one.

ideas.idea: The two key traits of a value investor are patience (enjoy watching paint dry) and circle of competence; the test for understanding is that if you have any doubt, you do not understand it.
ideas.detail: You must understand a business as well as the CEO, otherwise pass, put it in the too-hard file, or study until there is no doubt. Buffett told him he can only judge 4 of 100 people as really good and 4 as really bad and ignores the other 92; with 50,000 public companies you need only three or four to get rich.

ideas.idea: Value investing is a low calling that adds little to society, so he gives money away through Dakshana to make up for it.
ideas.detail: Asked whether buying undervalued shares exploits others, he agrees it is 'low quality but high income' work, and says a value investor improves the planet by giving the money away, likely doing a better job than the government.

ideas.idea: Knowing is not enough; conviction is shown by what percent of your net worth you put in, and position sizing is the hardest question after the decision to invest.
ideas.detail: A Goldman banker who did the Tencent IPO never bought a share. Guy Spier put only 0.2% of his $160 million fund into Maotai when Pabrai pitched it, while Li Lu (Yong Pingan) would have put 25%. Pabrai's own Maotai checklist: liquor company with a thousand-year brand, no competition, limited supply, and a fifth of the world's population rising.

ideas.idea: He bought GM warrants in 2012 rather than LEAPs because they had seven years of duration and distressed-era terms dictated by the US Treasury.
ideas.detail: US LEAPs max out at two years; the GM warrants could be handed to the company for stock at any time and were an instrument GM would never issue except under bankruptcy-era distress, so they were unusually attractive.
